title: Hounslow murder investigation launched as woman dies after fire
author: Jess Warren
content:
![A general view of Berkley Avenue in Hounslow.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/521/cpsprodpb/7d82/live/7d47bb80-9bf2-11f1-8470-d18257d2d589.png)
A 48-year-old woman died in hospital following a fire at a residential address in Hounslow
- Published
A murder investigation is under way after a 48-year-old woman died in a fire in west London.
Officers were called to a residential address on Berkeley Avenue, Hounslow, at about 01:15 BST on Wednesday following reports of the blaze, the Metropolitan Police said.
Six men and three women were taken to hospital, where the 48-year-old woman died. Another woman, 40, is in a life-threatening condition.
The Met said no arrests had been made but officers believed the fire may have been started deliberately. Det Ch Insp Neil John said: "Our inquiries are progressing at pace as we work to establish the full circumstances surrounding the fire."
John said the force's thoughts were "first and foremost with the victim's family and loved ones at this extremely difficult time, as well as everyone who has been injured".
The remaining seven people have been discharged after receiving treatment for minor injuries.
John said the force understood the incident to be isolated to a residential address, but officers would remain in the area and provide updates as the investigation continues.
A London Ambulance Service spokesperson said: "We were called at 01:18 BST today to reports of a fire on Berkeley Avenue, Hounslow.
"We sent resources to the scene including ambulance crews, a paramedic in a fast-response car, an incident response officer and paramedics from our hazardous area response team.
"We treated nine patients and took them all to hospital."
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: A murder investigation has been launched after a 48-year-old woman died in hospital following a residential fire on Berkeley Avenue in Hounslow. Police and emergency services responded to the blaze at about 01:15 BST on Wednesday, taking nine people to the hospital. Authorities believe the fire may have been started deliberately, though no arrests have been made at this time.
key_points: A 48-year-old woman died following a fire at a residential address in Hounslow.
A 40-year-old woman remains in a life-threatening condition in the hospital.
Six men and three women in total were taken to the hospital for treatment.
Police believe the fire may have been started deliberately, and no arrests have been made yet.
Emergency services including the Metropolitan Police and London Ambulance Service responded to the scene at approximately 01:15 BST.

title: Russia is threatening escalation against Britain: Here’s how they could do it
author: David Blair; Roland Oliphant
content:
“You send a message that you are capable of penetrating a Western airport and Western Europe, and potentially it might be extremely damaging, but you stop short of causing any real damage. That would serve the purpose, because the purpose we have seen since 2022 in Russian sabotage operations was always to raise the costs of supplying support to Ukraine and raising the costs of protecting critical infrastructure.”
Given that Russia is also doubtless seeking to divide British society and stir up as much trouble as possible, there are plenty of other methods that have already been tried elsewhere. In France, Russian agents have variously deposited pigs’ heads outside mosques, defaced synagogues and vandalised the country’s Holocaust memorial. They even left mock coffins under the Eiffel Tower. The French government has also blamed Russia for trying to frighten tourists away from Paris by spreading the story in 2023 that the city’s hotels were infected with bed bugs.
Many of those operations could be traced back to a Russian company called the Social Design Agency, which is close to the Kremlin, according to leaked documents published by Delfi, an Estonian news website.
Last month, British police officials warned that both Russia and Iran were trying their best to inflame social conflict. “Their ultimate goal is destabilising our democracy, sowing division and chaos, and disturbing our peace,” said Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism policing.
Assassinate Britons inside Britain
Likelihood: Medium
Russian intelligence has a long record of murdering – or trying to murder – people on British soil. But, so far, the targets have always been Russian exiles whom the Kremlin would consider traitors. The former spy Alexander Litvinenko, for instance, suffered an agonising death in 2006 when two Russian agents poisoned him with radioactive polonium in a London hotel. Later, in 2018, two GRU officers attempted to kill Sergei Skripal, a Russian defector, with Novichok nerve agent in Salisbury. Skripal survived, but his erstwhile assassins carelessly discarded their lethal substance, which killed Dawn Sturgess, an innocent British mother of three.
If Russia wished to escalate, it could expand its target list to include British citizens involved in arming Ukraine. Once again, events in Germany may provide a guide. In 2024, the CIA uncovered a Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger, the chief executive of Rheinmetall, the German defence giant.
His British counterpart would be Charles Woodburn, the chief executive of BAE Systems, the biggest British defence company and a supplier of advanced drones to Ukraine. But Woodburn – and others like him – will presumably be well-protected against any threat.
Indeed, killing people in Britain might be harder than doing so elsewhere in Europe. “It should not be completely ruled out, but Britain has built experience because of the Litvinenko and Skripal cases,” says Katia Glod, the deputy head of foreign policy at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre. “It’s harder to do that in Britain today than in Germany or France, which are probably more penetrated by [Russian] spies.”
Attack British facilities in Ukraine
Likelihood: High
This is probably the most likely option for any Russian escalation. Britain’s effort to supply Ukraine relies on a network of physical facilities inside that country. The existence of some has been publicly disclosed. In March, the Ministry of Defence said there were four “maintenance, repair and overhaul” facilities in Ukraine, where “UK companies with British and Ukrainian workforces” were engaged in reconditioning armoured fighting vehicles and artillery.
BAE Systems, meanwhile, announced in 2023 that it was establishing a “local presence” inside Ukraine. If Russia knows where any of these facilities are located, striking them with missiles or drones – and probably killing any Britons working inside them – would be a straightforward way of retaliating against Britain.
“They probably would try to start with something on Ukrainian territory,” says Soldatov. “They are actually quite creative at identifying what belongs to which country in Ukraine, so they might attack some facilities which they think might have some connections to Britain.”
What about British diplomatic premises, such as the embassy in Kyiv? Russia is less likely to take that step because it has plenty of embassies of its own and therefore retains an interest in preserving the immunity of diplomatic premises.
As for the drones that Britain is sending to Ukraine for long-range strikes on Russia, one option would be to target them as soon as they enter the country. Moskovsky Komsomolets, a Russian daily, recently pointed out that the drones in question are delivered as finished products and suggested targeting the containers the moment they crossed the border into Ukraine. That would require precise intelligence about the timing of drone consignments and the exact lorries in which they are carried.
Whether the Russians have acquired such detailed information is unknown. If they have, using this intelligence to destroy the British-supplied drones before they can take off would be the most logical response.
Direct military strikes on Britain with missiles or armed drones
Likelihood: Low
As Ukrainian attacks cripple oil refineries, giant warehouses and arms factories across Russia, the Kremlin must be sorely tempted to hit back against one of its enemy’s principal allies. At this moment, almost everywhere in Europe and particularly in Britain, advanced weapons are being made for Ukraine to use against Russian soldiers on the frontline and increasingly against targets in Russia itself.
Tempting but still unlikely. With its force bogged down in Ukraine and its arms-making capacity stretched to the limit, the last thing that Russia needs is to provoke a retaliatory attack from Nato. If a Russian missile or drone were to slam into a British arms factory, killing scores or hundreds of people inside, the danger is that Britain might invoke Article V, the mutual defence clause of the Nato treaty, and Putin’s difficulties would suddenly become even greater.
“I don’t think the military logic would allow that option,” says Glod. “I don’t think the Kremlin discounts the possibility of a Nato kinetic strike back and it wouldn’t be able to counter that because of its stretched military production.”
Despite the blood-curdling words of the Russian embassy in London – though it is notable that the threatening statement did not come from a higher level, such as the foreign ministry in Moscow or the Kremlin itself – the most likely outcome is that Russia will step up the existing campaign against Britain. Its operatives will probably do more of the same, running the gamut of sabotage, drone incursions, cyber attacks and disinformation, while staying just below the level of triggering open armed conflict.
“In many ways,” says Galeotti, referring to the embassy statement, “the language is an expression of impotence because, yes, Putin does have escalatory options, but they all have massive costs and risks for Russia.”
summary: Russia is considering potential escalations against Britain to raise the costs of supporting Ukraine and to destabilize British society through operations such as sabotage and disinformation. While methods like hybrid warfare, attacks on British facilities in Ukraine, or targeting UK-supplied weapons are possible, direct military strikes on Britain remain unlikely due to the risk of triggering NATO's mutual defense clause. Consequently, Russia is expected to continue utilizing covert tactics like sabotage and cyber attacks that remain just below the threshold of open armed conflict.
key_points: Russian sabotage and influence operations aim to raise the costs of supporting Ukraine and sow division in Western societies.
Potential escalation tactics include targeting British citizens involved in arming Ukraine or attacking British maintenance and repair facilities located within Ukraine.
Direct military strikes on British soil are considered unlikely because they risk triggering NATO's Article V mutual defense clause.
Russia is most likely to intensify its existing campaign of sabotage, drone incursions, cyber attacks, and disinformation.

title: Burnham hits back after Russia threat over Ukraine’s ‘use of British drones’
author: Athena Stavrou
content:
Andy Burnham has insisted Britain will continue to “support Ukraine 100 per cent” despite Russia threatening “consequences” for strikes made with British-built drones.
Russia’s embassy to the UK said reports that Ukrainian forces had used unmanned aircraft manufactured by two UK companies “confirm that London is deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis”.
It accused Britain of “seeking to contain Russia and inflict maximum damage on it by proxy” and warned that the deeper its involvement becomes, “the higher the price it will pay”.
“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” it said.
But the prime minister hit back, saying Britain would not be deterred by the threats. Asked what his message to Vladimir Putin was after Russia accused the UK of escalating the war, Mr Burnham said: “This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100 per cent against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin.
“We are providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself, and that’s been the British position all the way through this conflict by previous prime ministers.
![During a visit to Wolverhampton bus station, Andy Burnham was asked what his message to Vladimir Putin was after Russia accused the UK of escalating the war and warned of consequences](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/18/12/2026-08-18T112027Z_2032056839_RC2W0NAWW3SC_RTRMADP_3_BRITAIN-POLITICS-BURNHAM.JPG)
“It remains the case with me. We are not fair weather friends. We will be there in Ukraine’s hour of need, and that won’t change.”
His defiant stance comes after a government minister insisted that Britain would continue to supply Ukraine with military equipment and continue to “stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine”, despite Moscow’s warning.
Work and pensions minister Lilian Greenwood told Sky News on Tuesday: “The Russians should be clear that our resolve remains completely steadfast in backing our friends in Ukraine and providing them with the equipment that they need.
However, Russia’s warning has raised questions over Putin’s willingness to strike Britain, risking Nato intervention in Russia.
Andrey Fedorov, former deputy foreign minister of Russia, said there was a feeling in Moscow that Nato will not hit back at Russia, even if the UK is attacked.
“Taking into consideration current instability within Nato, current problems within Nato, it’s quite possible that Nato will do nothing,” he told BBC Radio 4.
“[It] will make a statement, or will use Article Four, but not Article Five. It’s linked first of all to Donald Trump, who is still the keeper of the keys in Nato.”
Former Tory defence secretary Grant Shapps told The Independent Nato “undoubtedly has genuine problems”, not least the political divisions within the West, but Putin “would be a fool to mistake disagreement for weakness in a moment of true crisis”.
He added: “Britain, France, Germany and Poland alone spend around $318bn a year on defence, compared with Russia’s $190bn, and I cannot imagine those countries standing aside if a Nato member were deliberately attacked.
“For all Putin’s rhetoric and bluster, his behaviour tells us something important: he still fears what Nato can do when it is stirred into action. His strategy has always been to divide, intimidate and test the alliance without triggering its overwhelming collective strength. He should be extremely careful not to miscalculate.”
![The Ministry of Defence underlined its support for Ukraine’s actions](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/18/07/13962173b1f9365e7b8041b044c55eaaY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MTE5NzMz-2.34417666.jpg)
Former foreign secretary Sir Malcolm Rifkind warned the UK “is a nuclear weapon state, which would make a Russian missile or drone attack a much higher risk for Putin than a non-nuclear weapon target state”.
He said he believed Nato would respond, adding, “On such a high-profile issue Trump would not veto Article 5 (which does not require that we go to war with Russia, but requires the allies to decide how to respond). Even if I am wrong, the rest of Nato (Europe plus Canada) would support the UK.”
Former national security adviser Peter Ricketts said: “This was a golden opportunity handed to a Russian propagandist to try to intimidate and divide British opinion, and he took it with gusto. The Russians have regarded us as a hostile state for many years and we have to expect their sabotage/subversion will continue. But we shouldn’t be spooked by Mr Fedorov.”
A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “Russia should be in no doubt about the resolve of this government to stand against Russian aggression, in Ukraine and against the UK and our allies.”
Kyiv has stepped up operations inside Russia this year, increasingly deploying long-range missiles and drone swarms against military industries and energy facilities.
It has also targeted giant depots for Wildberries – Russia’s largest online retailer – burning billions of pounds of merchandise and bringing the war home to the Russian public more than four years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Ukraine’s strategy of long-range drone strikes is believed to be aimed at cutting Moscow’s revenue for the war and making Russian citizens feel the impact of the invasion, with the attacks contributing to mounting economic damage.
It launched three times as many of those strikes in July as it did in January, according to data from Acled, an independent conflict monitor.
Repeatedly hitting deep into Russia has forced its military to stretch air defences over a larger area.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said on Saturday that it had shot down 598 Ukrainian drones over 19 Russian regions, as well as the Black and Azov Seas and the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea.
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has stated that Britain will continue to support Ukraine unconditionally despite Russian threats of consequences over the use of British-built drones. Russia's embassy accused London of escalating the conflict, but British officials and ministers reaffirmed their steadfast resolve to supply military equipment. While some analysts suggested Moscow might test NATO unity, former defense figures and officials emphasized that the UK is a nuclear power and that NATO allies would respond to any attack.
key_points: Andy Burnham insisted the UK will support Ukraine 100 per cent and will not be deterred by Russian threats.
Russia warned of consequences after reports that Ukrainian forces used British-manufactured drones.
Work and pensions minister Lilian Greenwood confirmed that Britain's resolve to back Ukraine remains steadfast.
Former officials debated whether Russia might miscalculate NATO's unity, noting the UK's status as a nuclear-armed state.
Ukraine has significantly increased its long-range drone strikes deep inside Russia to impact Moscow's war revenue.

title: Andy Burnham calls on wider society to help end homelessness by Christmas
author: Rowena Mason
content:
Andy Burnham has said government money alone may not be enough to get rough sleepers off the streets by Christmas, as he issued a “rallying call” for councils, charities and communities to help solve the problem.
Speaking on a visit to the north-east of England, he said he felt “very passionately” about tackling homelessness and wanted the wider society to play a part in wiping it out.
The prime minister acknowledged that not every rough sleeper might take the offer “for their own reasons”. But he said a nationwide effort to stop as much rough sleeping as possible by Christmas was the aim – replicating what happened in the Covid pandemic.
Burnham told reporters: “The government money may not fully get us there, and I’m saying to wider society, faith organisations, let’s see if we can do this together. Let’s see if Britain can do this. Give everybody an offer to come inside before Christmas. You know, that is just something we can do.
“We did it in the pandemic. We can do it again, and it’s a rallying call, really, that I’m putting out there today, with a lot of government money behind it.”
Burnham wrote in the Guardian on Tuesday that rough sleeping has become so common it now “feels like part of the scenery”, as he pledged another £100m to tackle the problem this winter.
The announcement puts tackling homelessness as a central policy for Burnham’s government, and gives voters a measure by which to judge his success.
![A row of tents outside the Midland Hotel in Manchester last year.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/23a5573cd8e3ddc77ae2197de10bcce506053f6e/0_0_8192_5464/master/8192.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham introduced schemes such as A Bed Every Night to offer emergency accommodation, but while the number of rough sleepers fell, it then began to rise again.
The prime minister said this was because “we were the only place providing that level of support, and understandably, people then travelled to Greater Manchester to access that support”.
He added: “So my point is, we can do this, but only if all areas are pulling in the same direction, and that’s what this funding is designed to achieve – to make this a nationwide initiative as we go into the Christmas period, getting everybody behind it.”
He said people being left to sleep on the streets “can often cost more to the state because people can be in and out of A&E, and in and out of hospital beds, and sometimes in contact with the police”.
As part of the national effort, Burnham said he would host a summit this autumn to “bring together leaders from across society – from business, finance, charities, health, faith communities and more – to ask what role each of them can play in ending rough sleeping”.
after newsletter promotion
![Andy Burnham stands in a grassy garden area with three women as one speaks as if she is explaining something. There are garden tools behind them and a brick wall by a large and grand-looking brick and stone building behind black iron railings.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/97a38a045f729d53f3a006d4f28f2f54ea3c352b/0_0_5304_3536/master/5304.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Burnham said on Wednesday that he would be donating 15% of the additional salary he gets as prime minister to homelessness causes.
Speaking to the Big Issue, he said he wanted to continue what he had been doing as mayor of Greater Manchester. He has already said he would donate 15% of the salary he gets for being an MP to local causes in his constituency of Makerfield.
He told the magazine: “For the best part of nine, almost 10 years, I donated 15% of my salary as mayor of Greater Manchester to tackling homelessness in Greater Manchester.
“I am making a commitment to donate the same of my prime minister’s salary. I’m donating part of my constituency MP salary to local organisations, but the extra bit that comes with being prime minister, I’m making the same commitment.
“I wouldn’t want to ask anybody to do anything that I’m not prepared to do. I want to lead from the front. This issue matters massively to me.”
The latest annual national statistics, published in February, estimated there were 4,793 people sleeping rough on a single night in autumn 2025 in England. This was a new record and the fourth annual increase in a row, with 43% of those people sleeping rough in London and the south-east.
summary: Andy Burnham has issued a rallying call for councils, charities, faith organizations, and communities to help eliminate rough sleeping by Christmas. Backed by £100m in winter funding and modeled after efforts during the Covid pandemic, the initiative aims to offer indoor accommodation to every rough sleeper nationwide. Burnham also announced he will host a summit this autumn and commit 15% of his prime minister's salary to homelessness causes.
key_points: Andy Burnham stated that government funding alone may not be enough to end rough sleeping by Christmas without a nationwide community effort.
A new £100m winter funding package is being deployed to encourage all areas to pull in the same direction and offer everyone a place to come inside.
Burnham will host an autumn summit bringing together leaders from business, finance, charities, health, and faith communities.
Burnham committed to donating 15% of his additional salary as prime minister to homelessness causes.

title: Family who drowned off Sussex coast were Palestinian refugees
author: Samuel Montgomery; Ben Adams
content:
![Zeina Alyan, Hossam El-Khawwas, daughter Sarah](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498852006_17871469703810_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwfSVWeZ_vEN7c6bHu2jJnT8.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Zeina Alyan, Hossam El-Khawwas, daughter Sarah](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498852006_17871469703810_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwfSVWeZ_vEN7c6bHu2jJnT8.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
A couple and their teenage daughter who drowned off the Sussex coast on Tuesday were Palestinian refugees.
The Palestinian embassy told The Telegraph that Hassan El-Khawas, his wife Zeina Alyan and their daughter Sarah had died at Shoreham-by-Sea. Their second daughter, Saja, survived but is in a critical condition.
A spokesman said the embassy had been in contact with El-Khawas’s brother, who lives in the UK, to offer its support.
He told The Telegraph: “I can say that the name of the father who died, his name is Hassan El-Khawas, and his wife, and a daughter. They are from Rashidieh camp, originally, in the south of Lebanon.
“They are Palestinian refugees ... this is considered a national tragedy, losing three British Palestinians at such a time.
“There is an uncle here, we were in touch with them to see if they need any help or assistance and we will follow up with the British authorities regarding the situation now.”
The embassy said it believed that all members of the family had British citizenship. The spokesman said: “The whole family is in a rough situation mentally – very, very bad.”
In an update on Wednesday afternoon police said the family travelled from their London home to visit Shoreham, and entered the water from the beach at Shoreham Fort around 2pm on Tuesday afternoon, before getting into difficulty.
They do not believe there was any third party involvement.
In a statement, the Palestinian Forum of Britain said it “mourns, with hearts that firmly believe in the decree and destiny of Allah, the passing of Mr Hassan El-Khawas, his dear wife, and their daughter, from Rashidieh Camp, members of the Palestinian community in Lebanon, following their drowning in the Sussex area.
“We pray for the swift recovery of their second daughter, who has been taken to hospital. We kindly ask anyone who knows the family to help us get in touch with their relatives, so that together we may fulfil our duty towards them.”
There was a huge emergency services response on Tuesday afternoon, with air ambulances, an RNLI lifeboat and Coastguard crews at the scene near Shoreham Fort.
![Emergency services launched a rescue effort after reports of people in difficulty in the sea off Sussex on Tuesday](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498829232_17871460558770_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqyuLFFzXshuGqnr8zPdDWXhbQKbwj1ZsnNMhuR7O6ySI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
On Wednesday, Andy Burnham warned of the dangers of open water swimming.
Asked during a visit to the North East on Wednesday if the Government needed to do more on water safety, the Prime Minister said: “Always.”
He urged people to be wary of cold-water shock and said: “The thing I can say today – and there is still, I think, a further heatwave to come in this summer period – it is just to remind people about the dangers of open water swimming.
“The coldness, even when it feels hot outside, it can shock people, and that can cause the difficulties. So people just need to remember that at all times.
“I do need to praise the emergency services, who I know were on scene very quickly yesterday. They’ve had a busy summer, but they were there and we thank them.”
He said the incident was “a real terrible family tragedy” and sent “best wishes and love to wider friends and family”.
![Emergency services brought the family's younger daughter to hospital in critical condition after she was rescued from the water](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498794624_17871460552052_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Joss Loader, who lives nearby and represents Shoreham Beach Residents’ Association on Adur District Council, told the Press Association: “There’s just a really strong sense of shock. Obviously, people are really concerned for the young girl.
“A small. tightly-knit community with a very deep sense of shock and that sense of disbelief you get after a tragedy because it has come out of nowhere.”
Shoreham beach is a spit of land with water on three sides from the River Adur, the estuary and the sea, and Ms Loader said she understood the “tragic events” had happened in the estuary.
“It’s school holidays and we have had a wonderful summer, so the beaches have been packed with families,” she added. “The weather was quite calm, not as hot as recent days, but it was a perfectly normal day.
“People swim from those beaches even in the winter, and generally it is considered as safe as the sea can be. You wouldn’t be swimming there and think you were taking a risk.”
Ms Loader said she had reminded people not to speculate and to allow emergency services to investigate before an inquest was held.
![Floral tributes are left at Shoreham after three members of the same family drowned](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/news/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498826774_17871460556271_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqdgCWekBzj8QW4EiFpyW50-weplzV6HTFc0mQ-xBD1Q8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Anna Peacock, 81, who lives near Kingston Beach, across the water from Shoreham Fort, said emergency services were on the scene very quickly.
She said: “It was terribly sad to know that, just across the road, people have lost their lives. People come down to swim, particularly in the summertime and I don’t think they realise there’s a rip tide along here.
“It’s very inviting to come to the sea – but the tide could carry you out in seconds, and I don’t think people have realised that.”
Tom Rutland, the Labour MP for East Worthing and Shoreham, said: “It’s too early to know exactly what caused yesterday’s trouble that led to the tragic deaths but I think there’s always more that can be done to educate people about water safety.
“I think people living by the sea broadly have a good understanding of the dangers it can pose, but we need to make sure that everybody in the country has that same knowledge, given that people love to come to the coast in the hot summers that we’ve been having.”
summary: A Palestinian refugee couple and their teenage daughter drowned after getting into difficulty in the water off Shoreham-by-Sea on Tuesday. Their second daughter was rescued and remains in critical condition in the hospital. Police stated that the London-based family traveled to visit Shoreham and entered the water near Shoreham Fort, with no third-party involvement suspected.
key_points: Hassan El-Khawas, his wife Zeina Alyan, and their daughter Sarah died in the drowning incident.
A second daughter, Saja, survived and is currently in critical condition.
The family originally from the Rashidieh camp in Lebanon were British citizens living in London.
Emergency services responded rapidly with air ambulances, RNLI lifeboats, and Coastguard crews.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham and local officials highlighted the dangers of open water swimming and water safety following the tragedy.

title: Train investigators find track defect on approach to site of Lewes derailment, initial report says
author: Live Reporting Edited by Neil Connor
content:
![A shot of the train tracks, and one section is slightly bent. There is a white square around this section to more clearly point it out.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/vivo/live/images/2026/8/19/ebb9f385-7bdb-4770-bc7f-ee79af8231a5.jpg.webp)
A track "irregularity" has been found on the rails where a train came off the tracks in Lewes last week, investigators have said.
The Rail Accident Investigation Branch has released its initial report, external into the derailment which took place on Thursday 13 August, the hottest day of the year. The derailment threw three carriages off the track and onto their side, injuring 30 people, two of whom are still in hospital.
Investigators said there was evidence of previous "track maintenance activity" in the area and there had been several reports of "rough riding" from passengers on other trains in the same location.
In a joint statement after the report was released, Lucy McAuliffe, Network Rail's route director for Sussex, and John Whitehurst, chief executive of Greater Thameslink Railway, said they were "very sorry that this happened on our railway" and promised to "carefully consider any recommendations arising from the investigation".
The next steps of the investigation will look at how the track was inspected and maintained, and the effectiveness of any measures designed to address risks of operating trains in hot weather.

The August 13 incident occurred on the hottest day of the year, throwing three carriages onto their side and injuring 30 people, with two remaining hospitalized. The Rail Accident Investigation Branch noted previous track maintenance and prior reports of rough riding by passengers in the same location.

title: Thunderstorm warning for UK after record-breaking heatwaves
author: Tom McArdle
content:
![A red brolly](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498838259_17871302700850_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqYP-yEHEhjtPCwS59j6sPb1PAFSRU2fbP_NGNfbzcbEA.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![A red brolly](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498838259_17871302700850_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqYP-yEHEhjtPCwS59j6sPb1PAFSRU2fbP_NGNfbzcbEA.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Thunderstorms are set to strike swathes of Britain after weeks of record-breaking temperatures.
The Met Office issued a yellow warning for thunder and heavy rainfall, covering the East Midlands, the North East, the North West, and Yorkshire and Humber, as well as parts of Wales and Scotland, from 7pm on Wednesday evening until 10am on Thursday morning.
Forecasters said that the stormy weather was likely to trigger travel disruption and flash flooding, as well as damage to homes and power cuts.
The cooler and wetter conditions come after the UK’s fifth heatwave of the summer, during which the hottest day of the year was recorded in Kew Gardens, west London, on Thursday, when temperatures reached 38.1C.
On Wednesday, London experienced substantial rain for the first time in nearly two months.
The Met Office had predicted that parts of the country would experience the “first meaningful rain for a long time” after the record-breaking dry weather left many areas facing water shortages.
Provisional data from the forecaster’s weather tracker showed rain sweeping in from the west before falling in London for several hours in the early hours of Wednesday.
The website showed rain hitting most of the city, where there had been no significant rainfall in some areas for all of July and August.
Weeks of hot, dry weather have led to several hosepipe bans and wildfires. More than 27 million people across England have had hosepipe use restricted.
On Monday, Wessex Water announced a hosepipe ban for the first time since the summer of 1976. The water firm said the temporary prohibition for its 1.4 million customers in Bath, Somerset, Dorset and Wiltshire would come into effect from midnight on Tuesday.
It said its water supply network was facing record demand because of hot conditions and no significant rain forecast.
Five heatwaves have hit Britain this year, with this summer set to beat that of 1976 and become the hottest ever. More than 70 per cent of England is in drought.
Water bosses warned that longer-term forecasts suggested that any respite offered by the rain would not end the widespread restrictions on use, which were based on longer-term forecasts.
On Tuesday, Thames Water told customers to take shorter showers after warning that reservoir levels were lower than usual.
The utility, which has 16 million customers, said its London reservoirs were 74 per cent full at the end of last month. The average at this time of year is 87 per cent.
The heatwaves have increased the water demand. Thames said customers across London and the Thames Valley used around 100 million litres more than normal each day during July’s hot weather.
![Brighton had some long-awaited rain on Wednesday](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498835930_17871302960770_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
![People on a pier in waterproof jackets, with the sea behind](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/19/TELEMMGLPICT000498835787_17871303717300_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Aidan McGivern, a Met Office meteorologist, said Wednesday would be a “very showery day” across Britain.
He added: “I suspect many people across England and Wales will at least enjoy the feel of some rain falling out of the sky during the next few days, but it’s not going to solve the drought situation overnight because we’re not expecting huge amounts, and it will be highly variable because a lot of it will come in the form of showers.”
On Wednesday, highs of 25C in London, 20C in Cardiff, 19C in Manchester and 16C in Glasgow were expected, according to the weather service.
summary: The Met Office has issued a yellow thunderstorm warning for parts of Britain following weeks of record-breaking heatwaves and dry weather. The incoming stormy weather threatens to cause travel disruption, flash flooding, and power cuts, but is unlikely to immediately resolve ongoing drought and water shortage issues. The recent hot conditions, including the UK's fifth heatwave of the summer, have triggered hosepipe bans affecting over 27 million people across England.
key_points: The Met Office issued a yellow warning for thunder and heavy rainfall across parts of England, Scotland, and Wales.
The UK experienced its fifth heatwave of the summer, with Kew Gardens recording a high of 38.1C.
Weeks of dry weather resulted in hosepipe bans for more than 27 million people across England, including a restriction announced by Wessex Water.
Over 70 per cent of England is currently in drought, and water bosses warned that incoming rain will not immediately end restrictions.
Forecasters predict the stormy weather could cause travel disruption, flash flooding, home damage, and power cuts.

title: Burnham pledges to get thousands of rough sleepers off streets for Christmas – UK politics live
author: Tom Ambrose; Matthew Taylor; Rowena Mason; Andy Burnham
content:
Andy Burnham talks to Hubar, a homeless person in London, as he meets rough sleepers with staff from The Passage Homeless Charity. Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty Images
Andy Burnham talks to Hubar, a homeless person in London, as he meets rough sleepers with staff from The Passage Homeless Charity. Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty Images
Burnham announces drive to get thousands of rough sleepers off streets for Christmas
Hello and welcome to the UK politics live blog.
Andy Burnham has pledged to work to “get everyone in for Christmas” as he continues to build on his policy to end rough sleeping.
Arguing in the Guardian that rough sleeping has become so common it now “feels like part of the scenery”, Burnham promised he would mount a Covid-style campaign to get everyone off the streets this winter.
The announcement solidifies tackling homelessness as a central policy for Burnham’s government, and gives voters a measure by which to judge his success – although without a concrete target for ministers to hit.
Homelessness campaigners welcomed the move, but warned more will need to be done to tackle the longer-term temporary accommodation crisis, which has given the UK the worst homelessness problem in the western world.
We see people bedded down in doorways and sat outside stations, carrying their lives in rucksacks and sleeping bags on their backs. And I think most people have the same reaction: this isn’t right.
It shouldn’t be happening here. But we’ve lived with it for so long that something that used to shock us now feels like part of the scenery.
He added:
We did it in the pandemic. We got people out of the cold because, as a country, we decided it had to be done. We can do it again.
That’s why the first thing I announced when I became prime minister was a commitment to end rough sleeping. Not to manage it, not to reduce it – but to end it. And today, we’re taking the first step in getting it done.
We’re putting £442m behind a national drive to get everyone in for Christmas.
The prime minister is expected to visit to a homelessness charity in the north-east later today.
Burnham confirmed a new partnership between the government and the West Midlands Combined Authority (WMCA) to take local control of bus services in the region. Burnham said the “absolutely massive” move would protect thousands of jobs, which were threatened after the parent company behind local operator National Express indicated it was leaving the market.
Burnham said “nothing of consequence” was exchanged when he was text messaging somebody impersonating Donald Trump’s chief of staff Susie Wiles. “All politicians are receiving these pressures and these challenges, but I did everything right. There was a minimal exchange of information of zero consequence, and it was quickly reported,” he told reporters.
Burnham said he will present findings on a review of the early release scheme in England and Wales when parliament returns in two weeks’ time. Justice secretary Alex Norris is drawing up plans to “maximise public safety and minimise the early release of prisoners”, the prime minister said.
The green energy entrepreneur and Labour donor Dale Vince has urged the prime minister to allow more drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea, in a reversal of his previous position. Vince, who has given more than £5m to Labour over several years, said he had told Andy Burnham that the Rosebank and Jackdaw projects should be approved as long as the oil and gas produced were subject to price controls to make them cheaper than energy imported from overseas.
Labour ‘could lose up to 50 seats’ to Greens if new drilling in North Sea approved
Matthew Taylor
Labour could lose dozens of seats to the Green party if the government allows new drilling in the North Sea, according to internal research shared with the Guardian.
Green party analysis suggests up to 50 Labour MPs – including key Andy Burnham ally Louise Haigh – could lose their seats at the next election if the government fails to make urgent climate action a priority or allows new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea.
The research found that voters in these key Labour v Green seats want “bold action” to tackle the climate crisis, which has contributed to record heatwaves, devastating wildfires and crippling droughts this summer in the UK – and say Labour MPs will pay the price if the demands are not met.
Rachel Millward, deputy leader of the Green party, said: “If Labour won’t be swayed by the science or the moral imperative to leave all fossil fuels in the ground, perhaps they will listen to the polling. The data is clear: voters want more from our government on climate change, and they certainly don’t want our new prime minister to back away from his party’s bare minimum commitments.”
Labour dismissed the claims, pointing out that since Burnham took office the number of seats the Green party is projected to win at the next election has fallen from 20 to seven.
Last month, Burnham, who has been tight lipped about the climate crisis since tacking office, said he would be “pragmatic” about oil and gas and that decisions on new drilling would be made “in due course”. “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is where does it come from,” he said.
Do not cut benefits for disabled young people, dozens of UK charities urge ministers
Rowena Mason
More than 40 of the UK’s leading charities have warned ministers against imposing tougher benefit sanctions or cuts on disabled young people, as the government considers how to encourage more young people into work.
The charities raised concerns that an imminent review of young people and work by Alan Milburn could bring in stricter eligibility rules for keeping disability benefits – or remove them altogether – as part of a wider plan to boost flagging youth job rates.
Nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds in the UK are classed as Neet (not in employment, education or training). Milburn has warned this is economically unsustainable and disastrous for a generation of young people.
In their joint letter to Milburn and Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, charity leaders warn cutting support or bringing in sanctions risks pushing thousands of vulnerable youngsters deeper into poverty and further away from employment.
The charities fear that a previous Labour government proposal for the health element of universal credit to be removed for under-22s with a disability or long-term sickness, saving around £300m a year, may be resurrected.
Milburn – a former minister in the Tony Blair government – has made it clear England’s welfare, education and skills infrastructure needs to be overhauled but has so far refused to be drawn on whether he will recommend specific cuts to benefits.
However, his interim report, published in May, argued that state support was too focused on benefit support at the expense of practical programmes to help young people into work, inadvertently “trapping” them on benefits.
Angela Rayner accused Tory frontbencher James Cleverly of “scaremongering” over rules for illegal traveller sites.
Rayner said the government is making the rules “stronger and clearer” around unauthorised developments.
Cleverly, the shadow housing secretary, claimed changes to national planning policy frameworks will make it easier for travellers to get sites “rubber stamped” retrospectively, “often when they’ve already erected permanent structures”.
The Tories have vowed to “crack down on illegal traveller sites”, as communities were being “forced to tolerate illegal encampments and breaches of planning laws”, as well as “antisocial behaviour and petty crime, by a small minority of travellers”.
Speaking to Nick Ferrari on LBC, Rayner said:
He’s building a straw man, because what we’ve actually done is made things stronger and clearer throughout the rules around unauthorised development, making it harder, making it really clear that people who try and do this unauthorised development are stopped from doing it.
We explicitly tackle any potential environmental damage and transport impacts, and we’re making it harder for people to get retrospective permission for development which was built intentionally without approval, which the previous government did nothing about.
So I think he’s trying to scaremonger at the moment, and I don’t think it’s it’s OK, what he’s doing.
I’ve always thought you can tell something about a country by what it learns to walk past. And, somewhere along the way, we’ve got used to seeing people sleeping rough on our streets.
We see people bedded down in doorways and sat outside stations, carrying their lives in rucksacks and with sleeping bags on their backs. And I think most people have the same reaction: this isn’t right; it shouldn’t be happening here. But we’ve lived with it for so long that something that used to shock us now feels like part of the scenery.
That’s not on the public. It’s on us as politicians. For decades, Westminster has treated rough sleeping like a problem to step around rather than solve. It’s a philosophy that took hold in the 1980s and came back full force in the era of austerity: this idea that rough sleeping is just a fact of life rather than something government has a responsibility to end.
I’ve never accepted that. Britain is the fifth largest economy in the world. We’ve built the NHS, developed life-saving vaccines and invented the world wide web. But it’s somehow beyond us to get our own people off the streets? I don’t believe it for a minute. We did it during the pandemic. We got people out of the cold because, as a country, we decided it had to be done. We can do it again.
That’s why the first thing I announced when I became prime minister was a commitment to end rough sleeping. Not to manage it, not to reduce it – but to end it. And today, we’re taking the first step in getting it done.
Rayner also insisted that it is not a demotion for the chancellor that No 10 North will be taking charge of driving economic growth.
Asked by Sky News whether it was a demotion for John Healey, Rayner said:
Not at all, no. The chancellor is working really hard with the prime minister, with myself and other cabinet colleagues.
You’ll have seen the statement that the cabinet made I think now two weeks ago, where we were really clear on our intent to put devolution and community empowerment at the heart of this government.
So we saw in Greater Manchester, where Andy had more powers, we saw the economy growing faster than the rest of the UK, and the prime minister said he wants to see that growth in every postcode.
She added:
So working with No 10 North around how we devolve and work with businesses, with local partners to drive that economic investment in local areas, because they know what their economy is like, they know what the challenges are that they face, but they feel powerless at times when the power is so centrally controlled in Whitehall.
And what we’re all saying, including the chancellor, is that we’re going to work with partners to ensure that they feel empowered in this process, so they can drive their local economies.
Housing secretary Angela Rayner defended Andy Burnham’s record of tackling rough sleeping in Greater Manchester, arguing that it is “really difficult to do in isolation”.
Asked by Sky News about rough sleeping numbers in Greater Manchester dipping but then rising again, Rayner said:
We’ve got to keep a relentless focus on it. I think that’s the message from both what happened at the pandemic and also what happened in Greater Manchester.
The other lesson from Greater Manchester is it’s really difficult to do in isolation. We saw the figures go down, but obviously then we drew in people from other areas into Greater Manchester who knew that there were an offer there …
But that real focus has to be driven continually by the government and by our partners, rather than it be a focus for a time-limited period or in just one location.
Rayner said she is “very confident” that enough accommodation can be found to get everyone off the streets by Christmas.
Speaking to Nick Ferrari on LBC, she added:
It’s not just about taking people off the streets, it’s about that longer-term and medium-term goal of giving them the support they need to then get them a more secure housing situation, to get them employment, to get them support if they’ve got mental health or addiction issues.
So it’s a real drive to not just, you know, get people off the streets this winter and to solve it, but then for us to come back again next year.
Because this investment is more about putting the foundations down to say it’s not just about making your streets look clean and nobody’s on them, it’s about giving people the support they need to really say we care.

title: South East Water says supplies restored to about 7,600 Kent properties
author: Cash Murphy
content:
![People from South East Water putting bottles of water from the water station into a blue car. There are five people in the image, and they are all wearing high-vis vests.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/0536/live/8cd32ea0-9ae3-11f1-b2f7-5d1639b20e22.jpg)
A water station in Cranbrook is open to help those experiencing supply issues
- Published
Drinking water supplies have been restored to about 7,600 properties in Kent which have been experiencing no water or low pressure, South East Water (SEW) has said.
More than 8,000 customers were affected by the latest supply disruptions, which SEW said was a result of prolonged hot weather, high demand, pipe bursts, and power issues.
The company said supplies had been restored to properties in Herne Bay, Rough Common and Blean, but urged all customers to use water for "essential" purposes only.
About 400 properties in Benenden, Cranbrook and Rolvenden are continuing to experience low pressure or no water and properties in Herne Bay might experience "intermittent supplies" later, SEW added.
![A sign at the water station in Cranbrook, Kent. The signs says: "We apologise for water service disription - stations open 7am-10pm. Average wait time is 30 min."](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/c905/live/24feaf40-9acd-11f1-ad7d-21d5090bbb0d.jpg)
SEW said issues were a result of prolonged hot weather, high demand, pipe bursts, and power issues
Mike Court, South East Water incident manager, said water levels in the storage tank that supplies Benenden, Cranbrook and Rolvenden remained "critically low".
He urged "all customers to continue using water for essential uses only today".
Residents had been told it could be a couple of days before their water supplies were restored, with some having experienced days of disruption.
A bottled water station has reopened at the Weald Sports Centre in Cranbrook, which has been the worst affected area alongside Benenden.
Other stations are open at:
- Sainsburys, Altira Business Park, Herne Bay
- Kavanagh Cinema, William Street Car Park, Herne Bay
- Sturry Road Park and Ride, Canterbury
- Wincheap Park and Ride, Canterbury
![Bottles of water being used to spell "Help Us" by residents of Benenden affected by an ongoing outage. There is a border of water bottles alongside the sign. Beneath the sign, the grass is dry and yellow after the summer heatwaves and dry weather. The sky above is dark with rain clouds.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/027f/live/9a6c0590-9afd-11f1-a27d-25dca26018ed.jpg)
About 400 properties in Benenden, Cranbrook and Rolvenden are continuing to experience issues
On Monday night, Benenden residents used the emergency bottles of water they had received over the previous days to send a clear message, which read: "Help Us".
Residents organised to meet out on the green to stage the protest, with resident Nicola Stanway saying people in the village wanted to be heard.
Among the properties in the village without water is The Bull Inn, owned by Lucy Barron-Reid, who admitted she was becoming "quite tired and worn down" by the situation.
She told the BBC: "As a busy village pub, it's really challenging trying to work out how we can trade without water.
"It's now getting a little bit hairy. We haven't had water since last Thursday and we're supposed to be opening our kitchen tomorrow. At the moment, we're having to debate whether we can do that."
Also affected is Benenden's Community Shop, which also serves as a cafe, where water supply remains a "lottery", according to manager Clare Jaques.
"We have water at the moment but the pressure is not great, we have no idea when it will work and when it won't," she said.
![The exterior of Benenden's Community Shop in Benenden, Kent. A number of customers are sat outside eating and drinking. A sign saying "Benenden's 10th Anniversary" can be seen in the image.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/afce/live/4ce98140-9b01-11f1-a27d-25dca26018ed.jpg)
The manager of Benenden's Community Shop, which also serves as a cafe, said the water supply remained inconsistent
SEW head of health and safety, Mike Pickard, said: "We completely understand how frustrating and upsetting it is to be without water, particularly when people are trying to look after their families, go to work and carry on with their daily lives.
"We apologise unreservedly for the persistent issues and disruption this ongoing situation continues to cause our customers."
Meanwhile, the water company is urging customers to treat its frontline teams with patience after it had reports of staff being threatened and vehicles being attacked.
Pickard stressed: "No-one should face threats, intimidation or violence simply for doing their job".
He added: "If our teams feel unsafe, they may have no choice but to leave an area."
On Monday, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said the situation was "simply not good enough."
A spokesperson said the company's new leadership "must now deliver a step change in performance, where customers' needs are prioritised".
SEW was the first water firm to issue a hosepipe ban this summer, having barred 850,000 customers in Kent on 3 July.
This ban was extended to parts of Sussex, Surrey, Berkshire and Hampshire about three weeks later.
Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.
summary: South East Water has restored supplies to about 7,600 properties in Kent, though roughly 400 properties in Benenden, Cranbrook, and Rolvenden continue to experience low pressure or no water. The disruptions were caused by prolonged hot weather, high demand, pipe bursts, and power issues. Bottled water stations have been opened in affected areas, and the company is urging customers to use water exclusively for essential purposes while addressing the ongoing outages.
key_points: Drinking water supplies have been restored to about 7,600 Kent properties, but about 400 properties remain affected.
The supply disruptions were caused by hot weather, high demand, pipe bursts, and power issues.
South East Water has urged customers to use water for essential purposes only as storage tank levels remain critically low.
Bottled water stations have been set up in locations including Cranbrook, Herne Bay, and Canterbury.
The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs called the situation simply not good enough.

title: Body found in Wylam river search for missing soldier Liam Potts
author: Caroline Briggs
content:
![Search and rescue team of four in the River Tyne in Wylam. Two are wearing red helmets, one has a yellow helmet and the fourth is in white. They are wearing red and yellow waterproof clothing and red lifesaver jackets. Each has a pole with which they appear to prodding into the water, which is a murky green. Beyond them and in the foreground are trees, shrubs and other vegetation.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/ce9d/live/f5fd15f0-9b27-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Search and rescue workers have been scouring the river
- Published
Police searching for a soldier who went missing after spending the night with friends say they have found a body.
Liam Potts, 22, who served with the Coldstream Guards, was last seen heading towards Wylam in Northumberland from Wylam Bridge at about 00:20 BST on Saturday.
Specialist officers from Northumbria Police's Marine Unit have now recovered a body from the River Tyne close to the bridge.
Det Ch Insp Sarah Robson said: "This is an extremely sad development and our thoughts are very much with Liam's family and friends."
Formal identification is yet to take place but Liam's next of kin have been notified and are currently being supported by officers, the force said.
Robson said: "I would like to thank all of our officers, partners and volunteers for their assistance throughout the searches, along with everyone who shared our appeals and contacted us with information.
"We would continue to ask that people respect the family's privacy at this tragic time."
Officers do not believe there to be any third-party involvement and a report will be prepared for the coroner, the force added.
![Rescue teams in hard hats and dry suits search the river Tyne in the Wylam area. The water is dark with foam swirling on the surface.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/8f3f/live/04414c20-9a52-11f1-bc7b-a36e7e7ea706.jpg)
Rescue teams have been searching the River Tyne
Police said they had received a report of a disturbance at a nearby premises and a subsequent crash on the bridge involving a vehicle and a group of pedestrians.
A man and woman, both in their 20s, were seriously injured in the crash.
Officers said Liam was on the bridge at the time of the collision but he was not in the vehicle, nor was he believed to have been injured.
Two men, aged 22 and 23, have been arrested in connection with the report and both have been bailed pending further inquiries.

summary: Police searching for missing 22-year-old soldier Liam Potts have recovered a body from the River Tyne near Wylam Bridge. Potts was last seen heading toward Wylam after spending the night with friends and was on the bridge during a prior vehicle collision involving pedestrians, though he was not believed to be injured. Formal identification has not yet taken place, but his next of kin have been notified, and authorities do not suspect third-party involvement.
key_points: Liam Potts, a 22-year-old Coldstream Guards soldier, went missing after spending the night with friends.
Specialist officers from Northumbria Police's Marine Unit recovered a body from the River Tyne close to Wylam Bridge.
Potts was on the bridge at the time of a prior vehicle-pedestrian crash that seriously injured a man and a woman in their 20s, but he was not believed to be injured in it.
Police do not suspect any third-party involvement in Potts's disappearance and death.
Two men aged 22 and 23 were arrested in connection with a disturbance and the subsequent crash, and have been bailed.

A damaged silver Nissan with a shattered windshield and debris around it was the focus of the police response.
Emergency services cleared the railway, allowing the station to reopen safely.

title: When the next UK heatwave could come after temperatures dip
author: Frankie Lister-Fell; Brendan McFadden
content:
The UK will finally see rain and cooler temperatures across the country after last week’s heatwave – but we may not have seen the last of the heat.
A long-range weather forecast from the Met Office suggests that while the rest of August will remain cooler and see more rain, higher temperatures could return as we head into September.
However, the much-needed showers could be short-lived. The Met Office predicts there is a “chance that late-season hot spells or heatwaves develop, especially in the south” in the first 12 days of September.
Shorts
“Temperatures are likely to be above average overall” during this period, according to the forecast.
Niamh Murray, operational meteorologist at the Met Office, said a September heatwave “can’t be ruled out” but that it was too soon to say “with any real confidence” if it will happen, as temperatures will naturally drop as we head towards autumn.
On Monday, “showery rain” was reported across Scotland and Northern Ireland, moving into parched regions of southern England in the evening.
“By the end of Tuesday, I think most places should have seen some rainfall,” Murray added.
Wildfire alert
Almost three quarters of England and all of Wales are now in drought following prolonged dry weather, and millions face restrictions on water usage.
The British Geological Survey said the UK’s groundwater levels were in “remarkable” health. But Met Office chief meteorologist Will Lang warned that autumn rains were unlikely to spell the end of the drought.
![A general view of a phone warning against lighting anything that could spark a wildfire, including barbecues, campfires, and fireworks with parched grass in the background. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called in the military, announced a ban on disposable barbecues and warned smokers not to risk setting light to tinderbox Britain as he scrambled to respond to the summer heatwave and wildfires. Picture date: Friday August 14, 2026. PA Photo. Photo credit should read: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA Wire](https://inews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308324575.jpg?w=644)
On Friday evening, UK residents were startled by an alarm and emergency alert sent to mobile phones warning of a nationwide threat of wildfires.
It urged the public not to do anything that could spark a blaze, specifically using barbecues, lighting campfires or setting off fireworks, due to the “serious risk”.
This was the first time the government’s emergency alarm system, set up in 2023, has been used to send an alert to the whole of the UK, with firefighters battling multiple wildfires.
![A drone view of burnt-out houses following a large grass fire which spread to several homes yesterday during the hottest day of the year, in Stourbridge, West Midlands, Britain, August 14, 2026. REUTERS/Temilade Adelaja](https://inews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308277428.jpg?w=644)
Last week alone, emergency services attended to wildfires in South Wales; Stourbridge, West Midlands; Goldenhill, Stoke-on-Trent; and Kettering, East Midlands. Fire crews are still tackling a blaze in the New Forest in Hampshire that broke out on 9 August.
On Friday, the number of wildfires recorded across England and Wales so far this year surpassed the total for 2025 – which was previously the worst year on record for wildfires.
The Rainham volcano
Parts of the borough of Havering, in east London, have been plagued with severe fires, with residents living in fear that their homes will be destroyed.
Fires have been a “daily” occurence in Havering this summer, Rainham resident Chris Read, 78, told The i Paper.
Read lives near a park that overlooks the infamous Launders Lane site – a former illegal landfill dump with contaminated waste that frequently bursts into flames, dubbed the “Rainham volcano“, but has never been cleared away.
Read said the fires were “getting really scary now. I think there’s one in the borough every day, sometimes twice a day.”
![Could there be another heatwave in the UK?](https://inews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308408649.jpg?w=644)
One fire two weeks ago came dangerously close to her house. She said: “There was smoke, the winds blowing it our way. it’s just a case of shutting the windows, shutting the doors, and hope to God the fire goes. It’s like being in prison.”
Military deployed to help firefighters
Andy Burnham launched a package of measures to respond to the wildfires, with retailers ordered to remove portable barbecues from the shelves, and the Army deployed.
Soldiers from a Gurkha regiment were pictured in South Wales digging firebreaks – strips of land cleared of trees and vegetation – to help prevent the spread of blazes.
![CARDIFF, WALES ??? AUGUST 15: (NO SALES) (EDITOR'S NOTE: This Handout image was provided by a third-party organization and may not adhere to Getty Images' editorial policy.) In this handout image provided by the UK Ministry of Defence, Soldiers from 10 Queen's Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment (10 QOGLR) digging out fire breaks within the woodblocks in South Wales on August 15, 2026 near Cardiff, Wales. Around 200 military personnel were deployed to South Wales following a request from South Wales Fire and Rescue Service (SWFRS) for logistical, operational and planning support as crews tackled ten large fires across the region. The personnel came from one of the UK's three standby battalions, held at high readiness to support emergency services and local authorities during major incidents. Personnel from the Queen's Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment, with headquarters support from 22 Royal Engineers. Around 100 personnel were initially deployed, with a further 100 expected to follow, demonstrating the Armed Forces ability to provide rapid support to civil authorities during emergencies. (Handout photo by Corporal Christian P Delice/MoD Crown Copyright via Getty Images)](https://inews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308441241.jpg?w=644)
![Could the UK be set for another heatwave?](https://inews.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307715520.jpg?w=644)
None of Britain’s 49 fire and rescue services currently has direct access to a firefighting aircraft or helicopter to drop large quantities of water.
The i Paper revealed that the UK does have RAF Chinook helicopters which are capable of dropping up to five tonnes of water at a time from a huge bucket suspended below the aircraft.
But these and their specialist crews are currently based at RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus on standby to help with wildfires on the island.
£65m support for farmers
The Prime Minister has announced a £65m package to support struggling farmers.
Of the funds, £50m will be directed towards supporting environmentally friendly food production, through the Sustainable Farming Incentive. The remaining £15m will go towards the construction of on-farm reservoirs to provide supplies during future dry summers.
A growing number of water reservoirs across the UK have reached critically low levels this summer.
Five are now classed by the Environment Agency as “exceptionally low” – including Wimbleball and Blagdon in Somerset, which are running at just 50 per cent and 54 per cent respectively.
summary: Following a recent heatwave and widespread drought, the UK is experiencing cooler temperatures and much-needed rain, though the Met Office warns that late-season hot spells could emerge in early September. The prolonged dry conditions have fueled a record number of wildfires across England and Wales, prompting the first-ever nationwide emergency mobile phone alert and the deployment of military personnel to assist firefighters. Prime Minister Andy Burnham also announced a ban on disposable barbecues and a £65 million support package for farmers.
key_points: The Met Office indicates that a September heatwave is possible, though temperatures will naturally drop as autumn approaches.
Almost three quarters of England and all of Wales are in drought, with autumn rains unlikely to immediately end the water shortage.
A nationwide emergency alert was sent to mobile phones for the first time, warning the public of a serious wildfire threat.
Soldiers, including a Gurkha regiment, have been deployed to help emergency services dig firebreaks and tackle blazes.
A £65 million support package has been announced for farmers, including funding for on-farm reservoirs to prepare for future dry summers.

title: Man in court over man's dog bite death in Wakefield
author: Emily Johnson; Phil Bodmer
content:
![Blue and white police tape cordons off a woodland pathway.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/0287/live/9d501050-9ac9-11f1-a74b-2f66a3b83590.jpg)
The incident happened on a disused railway line in Calder Grove, Wakefield, police say
- Published
A man has appeared in court charged with manslaughter over the death of a man who was bitten by a dog on a footpath in West Yorkshire.
James Judge, 55, was left critically injured in an altercation on a disused railway line off Blacker Lane in Calder Grove, Wakefield, at about 13:30 BST on Saturday and died in hospital at about 19:00 the same day.
Lee Ellis, also 55, of Calder Grove, appeared at Bradford Magistrates' Court on Tuesday charged with manslaughter and being in charge of a dog dangerously out of control causing injury resulting in death.
Ellis, who was described in court as a self-employed farrier, was bailed to appear at Leeds Crown Court on 16 September.
Rob Fones, representing Ellis, told the court there was "a verbal altercation in regards to right of way".
Georgina Fishwick, prosecuting, said an initial post-mortem examination had been unable to determine the exact number of dog bites to Judge.
Ellis was not asked to enter a plea to the charges, but Fones said he would be "taking the matter to trial".
Ellis, who appeared in the dock wearing a grey sweatshirt and tracksuit bottoms, wiped his eyes and nose with a tissue during the hearing.
A German Shepherd dog seized as part of this investigation is being held in police kennels.
summary: A 55-year-old man has appeared in court charged with manslaughter and being in charge of a dangerously out of control dog following an incident in Wakefield. James Judge suffered critical injuries from a dog bite during an altercation on a disused railway line and died later that same day in the hospital. The defendant, Lee Ellis, was granted bail to appear at Leeds Crown Court in September.
key_points: James Judge, 55, died in the hospital after being bitten by a dog during an altercation in Wakefield.
Lee Ellis, 55, appeared in court charged with manslaughter and having a dangerously out of control dog.
The defense stated there was a verbal altercation regarding the right of way.
A German Shepherd dog involved in the incident has been seized and is being held in police kennels.

title: Cambridge University vice-chancellor heckled at Jason Arday vigil
author: Mousumi Bakshi; Elliot Deady
content:
Prof Deborah Prentice attended a vigil in Cambridge city centre on Monday
- Published
The vice-chancellor of the University of Cambridge was heckled as she was seen in public for the first time since the death of former professor Jason Arday.
Prof Deborah Prentice attended a vigil organised by the campaign group Stand Up to Racism in Cambridge city centre on Monday evening.
Shouting from a signpost in the city's market square, one attendee called Prentice "shameful" for failing to attend another event organised by Arday's students on Sunday.
Prentice previously said the university was "deeply saddened" by the academic's death.
![Dressed in a black turtle neck and trousers, Jason Arday smiles at the camera in a BBC Radio 4 studio.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/ea6e/live/9024e850-988b-11f1-83ef-33838a09c7c1.jpg)
Jason Arday was found dead in Battersea, south London, on Friday
Arday, 41, was found dead at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.
He resigned from his role at the university earlier this month after facing allegations of plagiarism. He had denied the claims and, in one case, had been cleared.
Asked about the heckling at the vigil, Cambridge University said: "The vice-chancellor attended the vigil to pay her respects.
"She understands that this is a very difficult time for many people. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jason's family and loved ones, who have lost a father, partner, brother, uncle and son."
Concerns over media scrutiny
Arday's death sparked a debate over whether the media scrutiny was excessive or justified by his prominence.
Anger at the level of media coverage he had been subjected to was felt by many of the people who spoke to the BBC at the rally.
Addressing a crowd, Melanie Benedict, undergraduate president of Cambridge's students' union, said Arday had faced "disproportionate public scrutiny" which "would've been unbearable for anyone".
"The systemic issues that academics of colour have to face year on year have been highlighted by the tragedy of Jason's public treatment and subsequent death," they said.
![A woman - Milli Akehurst - looking at the camera with a neutral expression. She is wearing sunglasses and standing in front of a market, with a group of people behind her.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/3ad0/live/2faa4f50-9afd-11f1-a27d-25dca26018ed.jpg)
Milli Akehurst's son studies law at Cambridge
Reflecting on the press coverage, the National Education Union's Cambridgeshire secretary Abby Maddison said: "It doesn't feel right, what has been happening to him."
Milli Akehurst, whose son studies law at Cambridge, said: "It really saddens me the fact that as a black mother who has a son that comes hereâ¦ to see this happening is just heartbreaking.
"I think racism played a big part in [what happened to Arday]. He was cleared [of plagiarism], so why did it continue, and why were there so many articles within the last month or few weeks?"
![A crowd of people standing in a market square looking on as they are addressed by a speaker at a vigil.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/b95d/live/6a4c6c00-9afe-11f1-a27d-25dca26018ed.jpg)
Crowds gathered in Cambridge's market square as part of a vigil organised by Stand Up to Racism
Tachya Brobbey said she had been "very moved and very upset" that Arday had been "so trodden into the ground by the media".
"Clearly there was a disproportionate focus on him. We know there are others where there have been allegations that haven't had that amount of attention.
"Equally, I can see parallels with people like Caroline Flack where the media go for someone and destroy them. I think there are lots of layers to this but, yes, racism is a feature of it and it would be naive to think it wasn't."
![A woman - Shareena Howley - looking straight at the camera with a neutral expression. She is wearing a black sleeveless T-shirt and is standing in front of a row of shops and a takeaway food outlet.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/8deb/live/a044a520-9afe-11f1-a27d-25dca26018ed.jpg)
Shareena Howley held back tears as she spoke about Jason Arday
Shareena Howley, who had met Arday, said: "He was gentle, he was intelligent, maybe he did make some mistakes but did he really deserve that? Did he really deserve to be hounded to death?"
"He was about empowerment. He didn't shut the doors behind him, he said 'here's the ladder, I will pull you up'," she said, holding back tears.
The 54-year-old said there had been other Cambridge professors who had faced similar accusations: "Where was the press then?"
![A cardboard sign with the words "shame on the British media. Digital lynching" among floral tributes.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/e0ea/live/f96320f0-9afe-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Tributes were left in Trafalgar Square, central London, where another vigil was held on Monday
Plagiarism row
The plagiarism row began after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he had found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.
Cofnas's post had been terminated after a backlash to his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".
Cambridge had celebrated Arday's appointment as a young black professor, one of a tiny and visible minority in academia. Only 1% of professors in UK universities are black, making each appointment hugely significant.
The university's chancellor Lord Smith criticised the "racist feeding frenzy" around Arday.
Sir James Cleverly said he was angry about what happened to Arday, and the university establishment - not just Cambridge - should have "done the robust due diligence and checking that should happen with any senior academic appointment".
The shadow housing secretary said he felt Arday was used as "bragging rights by some universities".
On 6 August Cambridge announced an independent investigation into Arday's appointment.
It is understood the university does not feel it right to decide on whether to proceed with its investigation.
Stand Up to Racism also organised a vigil in central London on Monday, where several speakers criticised Arday's treatment by the media.
More than 100,000 people have signed a letter to the prime minister calling for a public inquiry into the media coverage surrounding Arday before his death.
Downing Street has since declined to say "at this stage" whether the prime minister was considering an inquiry.
